title: Foundations: Privateers - The Complete Guide
summary: What Privateers books are, where the genre came from, and how to read them.
body:
Privateers: Adventure is the literature of the far horizon: quests, voyages, and ordeals that test courage and ingenuity. Stevenson and Haggard wrote its charter; every expedition since follows their maps.

History: Defoe's Robinson Crusoe (1719) invented the survival tale. Stevenson (1880s), Haggard (1880s), and Verne made adventure the dominant popular fiction of the age of empire.

HOW TO READ THIS SHELF: start with the landmark titles below — each record carries the complete plot, themes, a quoted passage, and craft notes. Read foundations first, then follow the ladder: compounded titles deepen the form, advanced titles challenge it.

# Privateers foundations: reading-plan calculator
def reading_plan(total_pages, pages_per_day, days_per_week=7):
    days = total_pages / pages_per_day
    weeks = days / days_per_week
    return days, weeks

def session_words(words_per_minute=250, minutes=30):
    return words_per_minute * minutes

for pages in [200, 300, 400]:

print('30-min session at 250 wpm:', session_words(), 'words')

CRAFT NOTE: Haggard invented the lost-world genre in one book.

title: Robinson Crusoe (1719) - Complete Book Record
summary: Full record for Robinson Crusoe by Daniel Defoe (1719): complete plot, themes, passage, and craft.
body:
Robinson Crusoe by Daniel Defoe (1719). Shelf fit: The survival story.

COMPLETE PLOT: Crusoe is shipwrecked for 28 years, salvaging tools, building shelter, keeping a journal, taming goats - and finally rescuing Friday. A manual of self-reliance wrapped in spiritual autobiography.

THEMES: Work as salvation; the self made by labor.

FROM THE TEXT: "I learned to look more upon the bright side of my condition."

CRAFT NOTE: Defoe's inventory prose - lists of tools, stores, days - is the survival genre's DNA.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE PRIVATEERS SHELF: The survival story. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.
facts: Themes: Work as salvation; the self made by labor.

title: The Call of the Wild (1903) - Complete Book Record
summary: Full record for The Call of the Wild by Jack London (1903): complete plot, themes, passage, and craft.
body:
The Call of the Wild by Jack London (1903). Shelf fit: The dog's adventure.

COMPLETE PLOT: Buck, a California house dog, is stolen into the Klondike gold rush, learns the law of club and fang, and answers the wild - joining a wolf pack at the end.

THEMES: Civilization vs. the wild within.

FROM THE TEXT: "The toil of trace and trail was the expression of Buck's being."

CRAFT NOTE: London reverses the adventure: the hero goes native, and it's a triumph.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE PRIVATEERS SHELF: The dog's adventure. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.
facts: Themes: Civilization vs. the wild within.

title: Heart of Darkness (1899) - Complete Book Record
summary: Full record for Heart of Darkness by Joseph Conrad (1899): complete plot, themes, passage, and craft.
body:
Heart of Darkness by Joseph Conrad (1899). Shelf fit: The anti-adventure.

COMPLETE PLOT: Marlow journeys up the Congo to find Kurtz, the brilliant agent gone mad. Conrad turns the adventure inside out: the expedition discovers European savagery, not African.

THEMES: Imperialism's heart of darkness is European.

FROM THE TEXT: "The horror! The horror!"

CRAFT NOTE: Conrad's frame narrative makes the adventure a confession.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE PRIVATEERS SHELF: The anti-adventure. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.
facts: Themes: Imperialism's heart of darkness is European.

She by H. Rider Haggard (1887). Shelf fit: The immortal queen.

COMPLETE PLOT: Leo Vincey and Holly journey to a lost African kingdom ruled by Ayesha - 'She-who-must-be-obeyed' - a 2,000-year-old beauty. She steps into the flame of immortality and withers.

THEMES: Immortality as curse; love across millennia.

FROM THE TEXT: "She who must be obeyed."

CRAFT NOTE: Ayesha is adventure's first great female power - terrifying and magnetic.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE PRIVATEERS SHELF: The immortal queen. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.
facts: Themes: Immortality as curse; love across millennia.

The Coral Island by R. M. Ballantyne (1858). Shelf fit: The boys' adventure.

COMPLETE PLOT: Ralph, Jack, and Peterkin are shipwrecked in the South Pacific - battling pirates, befriending natives, learning empire's lessons. Stevenson called it his inspiration.

THEMES: Boyish competence; empire's playground.

FROM THE TEXT: "Ballantyne's boys: competent before they are grown."

CRAFT NOTE: Ballantyne's competence fantasy - every boy his own Crusoe.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE PRIVATEERS SHELF: The boys' adventure. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.

title: Around the World in Eighty Days (1872) - Complete Book Record
summary: Full record for Around the World in Eighty Days by Jules Verne (1872): complete plot, themes, passage, and craft.
body:
Around the World in Eighty Days by Jules Verne (1872). Shelf fit: The race against time.

COMPLETE PLOT: Phileas Fogg bets he can circumnavigate the globe in 80 days - by rail, steamer, and elephant. He wins by crossing the date line: the day he thought lost was gained.

THEMES: Precision vs. chaos; the world as timetable.

FROM THE TEXT: "Verne's world: grown smaller by steam and schedule."

CRAFT NOTE: Verne's timetable plot: the schedule is the suspense.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE PRIVATEERS SHELF: The race against time. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.
facts: Shelf fit: The race against time.
Themes: Precision vs. chaos; the world as timetable.

title: Treasure Island (1883) - Complete Book Record
summary: Full record for Treasure Island by Robert Louis Stevenson (1883): complete plot, themes, passage, and craft.
body:
Treasure Island by Robert Louis Stevenson (1883). Shelf fit: The pirate adventure.

COMPLETE PLOT: Jim Hawkins finds a treasure map, sails with Squire Trelawney's crew - infiltrated by Long John Silver's pirates - and survives mutiny, marooners, and murder to claim Flint's gold. Silver escapes with a bag of coins, winking at the reader.

THEMES: Greed vs. loyalty; the boy becoming a man.

FROM THE TEXT: "Fifteen men on the dead man's chest - yo-ho-ho, and a bottle of rum!"

CRAFT NOTE: Stevenson's rule: every chapter ends with the reader needing the next.

WHY IT BELONGS ON THE PRIVATEERS SHELF: The pirate adventure. Its influence runs through everything shelved here.
facts: Themes: Greed vs. loyalty; the boy becoming a man.

title: The Chapter-End Hook - Privateers Craft Study
summary: Craft study for Privateers writers and readers: the chapter-end hook.
body:
The Chapter-End Hook.

Stevenson's law: never end a chapter at rest. End mid-peril, mid-revelation, mid-escape.

Applied to Privateers: the principles above are the difference between a shelf of books and a pile of pages. Study the landmark titles on this shelf with these tools in hand.
